### **Equal Protection: Disparate Impact, Discriminatory Application, and Racial Proxies**

**High-Level Overview**

* A facially neutral government action generally violates **equal protection** only when it has both a **discriminatory impact** and a **discriminatory purpose**; foreseeable consequences alone ordinarily do not establish the required purpose.
* A plaintiff may prove **discriminatory purpose** from the **totality of the relevant facts**, but must show that the government acted **because of**, rather than merely **in spite of**, the racial consequences.
* A facially neutral classification may receive race-based treatment when it functions as a **proxy for race**, although cases involving language, ancestry, political affiliation, and grooming demonstrate that courts apply this concept unevenly.
* A neutral law may violate **equal protection** if officials apply it discriminatorily, but broad statistical disparities usually do not establish that racial discrimination affected a particular criminal proceeding.
* **Professor’s Tip:** The exam will be three hours, fully secure on the student’s computer, and **open book**. Students should nevertheless prepare a concise outline because there will not be enough time to search extensive materials during the exam.

**Disparate Impact and Discriminatory Purpose: Governing Framework**

1. Identify whether the government action contains an express **racial classification** or is **facially neutral**.
1. If the action is facially neutral, determine whether it produces a **disparate impact** on a racial group.
1. Determine whether the plaintiff can prove a **discriminatory purpose** from the **totality of the relevant facts**.
1. The plaintiff must show that the government acted **because of**, not merely **in spite of**, the disparate racial consequences.
1. If the plaintiff proves that discrimination was one purpose among several in a **mixed-motive** case, the burden shifts to the government on **causation**: the government must show that it would have taken the same action without the discriminatory purpose.
1. If no discriminatory purpose is established, the facially neutral action receives only **rational basis review**.
* This constitutional framework differs from the lecture’s account of **Title VII** employment cases. Under **Title VII**, proof of disparate impact may shift the burden to the employer; under constitutional **equal protection**, disparate impact alone does not shift the burden.
* Justice Stevens’s alternative conception of intent would presume that people intend the expected and entirely foreseeable consequences of their conduct. The professor emphasized that this view is not the prevailing one; modern doctrine demands a more purposeful showing of intent.

**_Griggs v. Duke Power Co._ (1971)**

* **Context and Rule**
  * This **Title VII** employment case raised hopes that courts would use a similar disparate-impact framework in constitutional **equal protection** cases.
  * The lecture described the case as holding that when a plaintiff showed that a facially neutral employer action had a racially disparate impact, the burden shifted to the employer to show that it lacked a discriminatory purpose.
  * The constitutional doctrine ultimately did not adopt this disparate-impact-triggered burden shift.

**_Washington v. Davis_, U.S. Supreme Court**

* **Facts**
  * A police department used a verbal-ability test in selecting applicants.
  * The plaintiffs presented evidence that the test disproportionately excluded Black applicants.
  * They also argued that the questions relied heavily on a cultural frame of reference that white applicants were more likely to possess.
* **Issue**
  * Does a facially neutral government action that produces a racial **disparate impact** violate **equal protection** without proof of a **discriminatory purpose**?
* **Holding**
  * No. A racial **disparate impact**, standing alone, does not establish an **equal protection** violation; the plaintiff must also prove **discriminatory purpose**.
* **Reasoning**
  * The governing inquiry is not merely whether the government could foresee the racial consequences.
  * The plaintiff must establish purposeful discrimination, meaning that the government acted **because of**, rather than merely **in spite of**, those consequences.
  * Without discriminatory purpose, the government action receives **rational basis review**.
* **Concurrences/Dissents**
  * Justice Stevens argued in dissent that courts should understand intent through the ordinary presumption that people intend the expected results of their acts.
  * He stressed the difficulty of proving the subjective motivations of one individual, much less the collective motivations of a legislature.
  * Under his approach, an entirely foreseeable discriminatory consequence could support a presumption of intent.
  * The professor emphasized that Justice Stevens’s approach has little present doctrinal traction; the majority’s more demanding conception of purpose governs.

**_Personnel Administrator v. Feeney_**

* **Rule**
  * **Discriminatory purpose** is evaluated from the **totality of the relevant facts**.
  * The challenged action must have been taken **because of**, not merely **in spite of**, its adverse consequences for the affected group.
* **Mixed Motives**
  * If discrimination was one of multiple purposes, the plaintiff first must establish that discriminatory purpose.
  * The burden then shifts to the government to prove that the challenged action would have occurred even without that purpose.
  * The burden therefore does not shift merely upon proof of disparate impact; it shifts later, at the **causation** stage.

**_Village of Arlington Heights v. Metropolitan Housing Development Corp._**

* **Facts**
  * The case concerned a zoning decision that disproportionately affected minority groups.
  * The professor was uncertain whether the affected plaintiffs included groups in addition to Black plaintiffs.
* **Holding**
  * Once the plaintiffs showed that discrimination was one purpose of the zoning decision, the government had an opportunity to show that it would have adopted the same decision even without that purpose.
* **Reasoning**
  * The case illustrates the distinction between proving a **discriminatory purpose** and proving **but-for causation**.
  * A plaintiff must first establish that discrimination was among the government’s purposes.
  * The burden then shifts to the government to show that the discriminatory motive did not change the outcome.

**Racial Proxies: Language and Ancestry**

* A facially neutral classification may be challenged as a **proxy for race** when it closely tracks racial identity.
* The cases discussed in the lecture show that correlation with race is not automatically enough: courts ask whether the classification itself is treated as racial and whether there is evidence of purposeful racial discrimination.
* A direct “smoking gun,” such as an admission that a neutral criterion was selected to exclude a racial group, would strongly support a finding of **discriminatory purpose**.
* The doctrine creates a recurring tension: a classification may be closely associated with race and produce a predictable racial result while still being accepted as a legitimate neutral criterion.

**_Hernandez v. New York_**

* **Facts**
  * During a criminal trial, the prosecutor used **peremptory challenges** to remove bilingual Latino prospective jurors.
  * The defendant contended that bilingual or Spanish-language ability was being used as a **proxy for race** to remove Latinos from the jury.
  * The prosecutor responded that the concern was not ethnicity or Spanish-language ability itself.
  * Instead, the prosecutor feared that bilingual jurors would rely on their own understanding of Spanish-speaking witnesses rather than the official interpreter’s translation, potentially biasing the proceeding.
* **Issue**
  * Did the prosecutor’s use of bilingual language ability as the basis for the strikes constitute purposeful racial discrimination?
* **Holding**
  * No. The stated concern about jurors independently interpreting witness testimony was accepted as a nonracial reason, and bilingual language ability was not treated as a **proxy for race** on the supplied facts.
* **Reasoning**
  * The defendant could not show that the prosecutor acted with a racially discriminatory purpose.
  * A “smoking gun” statement that bilingualism was being used to exclude all Latino jurors would have supported a different result.
  * Without such evidence, the prosecutor’s explanation was treated as valid even though the strikes could remove all Latino jurors.
  * The case demonstrates the high evidentiary bar for proving that a facially neutral explanation for a **peremptory challenge** is racial pretext.

**_Rice v. Cayetano_**

* **Facts**
  * Land formerly held by Hawaii’s royal family was held in trust for Native Hawaiians.
  * The **Office of Hawaiian Affairs** administered the trust.
  * Eligibility to vote for the Office’s trustees was limited through an ancestry requirement tied to having an ancestor in the Hawaiian Islands at the time of the conquest.
  * The restriction was intended to protect the remaining land base of Native Hawaiians.
* **Issue**
  * Was the ancestry-based voting qualification an impermissible **racial classification** or **proxy for race**?
* **Holding**
  * Yes. The ancestry qualification was treated as a **proxy for race**.
* **Reasoning**
  * The case’s central complication was whether Native identity should be understood as a **racial classification** or a **political classification**.
  * The Court did not simply declare that all Native identity is racial.
  * It instead equated the particular ancestry qualification with race, treating ancestry as the racial proxy in this setting.
  * The result can be characterized as operating in the opposite direction from many discrimination claims because the challenged classification was designed to protect Native Hawaiian interests and land rather than subordinate the covered group.
* **Exam Significance**
  * The case illustrates that ancestry can be treated as a racial proxy even where the government’s objective is protective or remedial.
  * The professor indicated that the case would reappear in the discussion of **affirmative action**.

**Racial Motivation Without Disparate Impact**

* The lecture framed **Palmer v. Thompson**, **Washington v. Davis**, and **Gomillion v. Lightfoot** together as supporting a general requirement of both **discriminatory purpose** and **discriminatory impact**.
* A racially motivated government action may survive if its operative effect is formally the same for everyone.
* This reasoning creates tension with cases rejecting the claim that formally symmetrical racial burdens are necessarily equal.
* A possible distinction is whether the challenged government action is facially neutral or expressly classifies by race.
* Financial explanations can also supply a neutral rationale that helps the government defend an action otherwise associated with racial avoidance.

**_Palmer v. Thompson_ (1971)**

* **Facts**
  * A southern jurisdiction closed public swimming pools rather than integrate them.
  * Similar tactics during the 1960s included closing public services and, in some places, entire school districts to avoid integration.
  * The closure affected Black and white residents in the same formal manner because no one could use the pools.
  * The government also offered financial explanations for the closure.
* **Issue**
  * Does a racially motivated closure violate **equal protection** when the closure has no disproportionate operative effect on Black residents?
* **Holding**
  * No. The closure was upheld because it affected Black and white residents identically and therefore lacked the necessary discriminatory effect.
* **Reasoning**
  * The Court accepted that the action may have involved a bad racial motive but emphasized the absence of a disproportionate impact.
  * The action was facially neutral: the government closed the pool rather than expressly assigning access according to race.
  * The Court distinguished **Gomillion** as resting on the actual effect of the challenged enactment rather than merely the motivation behind it.
  * The professor read **Palmer** together with **Washington v. Davis** to suggest that purpose without impact is insufficient, just as impact without purpose is insufficient.
* **Counterarguments**
  * The result appears inconsistent with the spirit of **Loving v. Virginia**, where formally equal prohibitions on interracial marriage could not save an express racial classification.
  * It also echoes the rejected “separate but equal” logic associated with **Brown v. Board of Education**: formal symmetry can obscure the racial nature of government action.
  * The cases may be distinguished because the laws in **Loving** and **Brown** expressly referred to race, while the pool closure did not.
  * The government’s financial rationale supplied an additional ostensibly neutral explanation.

**Discriminatory Application of Facially Neutral Laws**

* A law may be neutral on its face and may even have been enacted without a discriminatory motive, yet violate **equal protection** when officials administer it only against a racial group.
* **Discriminatory application** focuses on the government’s actual pattern of enforcement rather than solely on the text or the original drafters’ motivation.
* An almost perfectly one-sided enforcement pattern can make discriminatory administration easier to infer than a statistical disparity affecting, but not fully separating, racial groups.

**_Yick Wo v. Hopkins_, U.S. Supreme Court**

* **Facts**
  * The case arose during an era of extensive anti-Chinese federal, state, and local legislation, only four years after the Chinese Exclusion Act.
  * California measures included a foreign-miners license imposed on persons not born in the United States; a facially neutral San Francisco ban on carrying laundry on a shoulder pole, a method associated with Chinese workers; a facially neutral ban on long braids known as the queue ordinance; school-segregation laws; and express exclusion laws naming groups, including so-called “Mongolians.”
  * The challenged local laundry ordinance prohibited operating a laundry in a wooden building, allowing laundries in brick or stone buildings.
  * Officials applied the ordinance discriminatorily against Chinese applicants.
* **Issue**
  * Can discriminatory enforcement of a facially neutral law violate **equal protection** regardless of whether the law’s drafters intended that discriminatory application?
* **Holding**
  * Yes. A facially neutral rule may be struck down when officials apply it only to one group or otherwise administer it discriminatorily.
* **Reasoning**
  * The decisive point was the ordinance’s discriminatory application, not whether discriminatory administration was part of the drafters’ original design.
  * Although the professor suggested that the discriminatory result almost certainly was intended, proof of that original intent was not necessary to the rule.
  * The nearly complete racial pattern of enforcement made the inference of discrimination substantially stronger than the less complete statistical disparity later presented in **McCleskey v. Kemp**.
* **Significance**
  * The case established a foundational rule against **discriminatory application of a facially neutral law**.
  * It is especially notable because it protected Chinese immigrants during a period otherwise marked by extensive anti-Chinese legislation.

**Racial Gerrymandering: Purpose, Effect, and Partisanship**

* A facially neutral redistricting decision can violate **equal protection** when boundaries are drawn with both the purpose and effect of excluding Black voters.
* The professor rejected the suggestion that the distinction between **Gomillion** and **Palmer** rests primarily on the **Fifteenth Amendment** rather than the **Fourteenth Amendment**. The cases instead emphasize discriminatory effect and purpose.
* Modern redistricting cases place **Gomillion** under pressure without expressly overruling it.
* Race and political affiliation are highly correlated in many areas, but courts do not automatically treat **partisan gerrymandering** as a **proxy for racial gerrymandering**.
* A strange district shape does not by itself establish the racial purpose required for **strict scrutiny**.
* A separate unresolved line of cases concerns districts designed to enhance minority representation; the professor indicated that this issue would be revisited after the **affirmative action** cases.

**_Gomillion v. Lightfoot_, U.S. Supreme Court (1960)**

* **Facts**
  * Officials redrew the boundaries of Tuskegee, Alabama, into an unusual shape designed to remove Black voters from the town.
  * The boundary change was facially neutral but had the effect of excluding Black voters.
* **Issue**
  * Did the racially motivated and discriminatory redrawing of municipal boundaries violate constitutional **equal protection**?
* **Holding**
  * Yes. The redistricting infringed the **Fourteenth Amendment Equal Protection Clause**.
* **Reasoning**
  * The case rested on the actual effect of the enactment: Black voters were removed from the municipality.
  * The decision therefore differs from **Palmer**, where the pool closure formally affected Black and white residents alike.
  * Read together with **Washington v. Davis**, the lecture’s synthesis is that a plaintiff generally must show both discriminatory effect and discriminatory purpose.
  * The mathematical extremity of the district’s effect could also suggest intent, illustrating the practical difficulty of fully separating purpose from effect.
* **Current Status**
  * The professor stated that **Gomillion** remains good law and has not been expressly overruled.
  * Its force has nevertheless come under pressure from more recent racial-gerrymandering decisions.

**_Underwood v. Hunter_**

* **Context and Rule**
  * The challenged provision disenfranchised people convicted of misdemeanors involving **moral turpitude**.
  * The rule had both a racially discriminatory purpose and a racially discriminatory effect.
  * The case supports the requirement that a facially neutral voting rule is unconstitutional when both purpose and effect are established.

**_Abbott v. Perez_, U.S. Supreme Court**

* **Facts**
  * Following the 2010 census, the Texas legislature adopted a redistricting map in 2011.
  * The district at issue extended from Austin toward San Antonio and had an unusual shape.
  * The 2011 map was found to be racially motivated and was struck down.
  * After an intervening court decree, the 2013 legislature readopted the map.
* **Issue**
  * Could the discriminatory purpose attributed to the 2011 legislature be imputed to the 2013 legislature when it readopted the map?
* **Holding**
  * No. The Court concluded that it could not find that the 2013 legislature acted with the discriminatory purpose attributed to the earlier legislature, and it upheld the district.
* **Reasoning**
  * The original map’s racial motivation did not automatically establish the later legislature’s purpose.
  * Intervening events, including a court decree and legislative readoption, prevented the Court from imputing the 2011 legislature’s motive to the 2013 legislature.
  * The Court declined to approach the modern legislature with the assumptions about racial purpose that might have applied during the **Jim Crow** era.
  * Political affiliation, although correlated with race, was not treated as an automatic racial proxy.
* **Criticism and Uncertainty**
  * Critics characterized the process as “map laundering”: a map initially found discriminatory passed through judicial and legislative proceedings and emerged substantively unchanged but without an attributable discriminatory purpose.
  * The professor was uncertain about the exact content of the intervening court decree and cautioned that the procedural details were complicated.
  * The lecture referred inconsistently to the year of the later legislative action; the supplied account otherwise identified the operative readoption as occurring in 2013.

**Recent Emergency-Docket Redistricting Decision: Unidentified Case**

* The lecture referenced a redistricting case decided during the current term but did not provide its name.
* The case involved unusual **mid-decade redistricting** and reached the Court through the **emergency docket**.
* An unsigned and very short opinion characterized the map as **partisan redistricting**, not racially motivated redistricting.
* Because of the abbreviated emergency-docket disposition, the lecture noted that little was known about the Court’s reasoning.
* The decision further illustrates judicial reluctance to infer a racial purpose from political line-drawing, even where race and partisanship are closely correlated.

**Peremptory Challenges and Racial Exclusion from Juries**

* During **voir dire**, prosecutors and defense attorneys question prospective jurors about possible biases, including experiences with police, views about police, family members’ experiences, occupations, and legal knowledge.
* A **challenge for cause** removes a prospective juror for an identified reason, such as bias for or against police.
* A **peremptory challenge** traditionally permits removal without stating a reason, and jury consultants may use demographic or other data to predict whether a juror will favor the prosecution or defense.
* Race may not be used as the basis for a **peremptory challenge**, but the prosecutor has substantial room to offer another explanation.
* The ease of supplying nonracial explanations makes **Batson challenges** difficult, as illustrated by **Hernandez v. New York**.
* **Public Policy:** Eliminating peremptory challenges entirely would remove a tool that can facilitate racial exclusion, though it would also eliminate a mechanism both sides use to remove jurors they suspect may be unfavorable without proving cause.

**_Batson v. Kentucky_**

* **Holding**
  * Attorneys may not use **peremptory challenges** to remove prospective jurors on the basis of race.
* **Reasoning and Application**
  * A prosecutor may defend a challenged strike by offering a reason other than race.
  * Because virtually any nonracial reason may suffice, proving that the explanation is a pretext for racial exclusion is difficult.
  * A prosecutor can therefore sometimes avoid a successful **Batson challenge** even when the strikes remove every member of a racial group from the jury.
* **Concurrences/Dissents**
  * Justice Marshall argued in dissent that **peremptory challenges** should be abolished entirely.
  * His approach responded to the practical difficulty of policing the true reasons behind nominally discretionary strikes.

**Statistical Evidence and Equal Protection in Capital Sentencing**

* Under **Washington v. Davis**, system-wide racial disparities do not alone prove that a decisionmaker intentionally discriminated in a particular defendant’s case.
* Statistical proof presents a **correlation-versus-causation** problem: a study may establish a powerful disparity without identifying the cause or proving discriminatory treatment in an individual proceeding.
* The more decentralized the challenged decisions are—such as decisions made by separate juries—the harder it is to attribute the aggregate disparity to a common discriminatory purpose.
* **Public Policy:** Accepting broad statistical proof could expose every stage of the criminal process, from policing and arrest through charging and sentencing, to discrimination challenges.
* **Countervailing Policy:** Refusing to consider strong statistical proof may insulate systemic and implicit racial discrimination precisely because an individual “smoking gun” is rarely available.
* Historical evidence can strengthen an inference from statistics by showing that the observed disparity accords with a longstanding system of explicit racial discrimination.

**_McCleskey v. Kemp_, U.S. Supreme Court (1987)**

* **Facts**
  * The case challenged Georgia’s administration of the death penalty during a period when large-scale statistical studies were examining racial discrimination in capital sentencing.
  * The death penalty previously had been halted across the country for a period during the 1970s because it was found to be administered in a racially discriminatory manner.
  * McCleskey argued that Georgia’s racially discriminatory capital-sentencing system denied him **equal protection** by making him more likely to receive a death sentence.
  * The **Baldus study** examined both the race of the defendant and the race of the victim.
  * A defendant convicted of killing a white victim was 4.3 times more likely to receive a death sentence than a defendant convicted of killing a Black victim.
  * The group most likely to receive a death sentence consisted of Black defendants convicted of killing white victims.
  * The largest disparity was associated with the victim’s race rather than the defendant’s race.
* **Issue**
  * Does statistical evidence of substantial racial disparities in Georgia’s capital-sentencing system establish that McCleskey was subjected to purposeful racial discrimination in violation of **equal protection**?
* **Holding**
  * No. The broad statistical evidence did not prove that racial bias affected the decisionmakers in McCleskey’s individual case.
* **Reasoning**
  * **Washington v. Davis** required proof of **discriminatory purpose**, not merely a substantial disparate impact.
  * General statistics concerning Georgia’s system could not establish causation or intentional discrimination in McCleskey’s particular proceeding.
  * Individual juries made the relevant sentencing decisions, making a common purpose harder to prove than in a case involving a single law or administrative policy.
  * Unlike the nearly complete disparity in **Yick Wo**, Georgia’s system still sentenced white defendants to death; the study did not show a 100% racial division.
  * The study’s strongest result concerned the victim’s race, making it more difficult for McCleskey to frame the disparity as discrimination against him because of his own race.
  * The majority feared that accepting McCleskey’s reasoning would call into question the principles underlying the entire criminal justice system.
  * Similar statistical challenges could be brought against other penalties and every stage of criminal administration, including policing and arrest.
* **Concurrences/Dissents**
  * Justice Brennan characterized the majority’s systemic concern as a “fear of too much justice.”
  * He argued that opening other criminal-justice decisions to scrutiny was not an adequate reason to reject a meritorious constitutional claim.
  * He emphasized the long history of explicit racism in the criminal legal system.
  * Courts should ask whether the conclusion suggested by statistical evidence is consistent with “our understanding of history and human experience.”
  * He relied on the legacy of a **race-conscious criminal justice system** and the Court’s own recognition that racial attitudes persistently threaten criminal proceedings.
* **Policy Debate**
  * Statistical studies can contain methodological uncertainties and may demonstrate correlation rather than causation.
  * Nevertheless, statistics may be among the strongest available forms of proof where discrimination is implicit or dispersed across many decisionmakers.
  * The case reflects a choice to demand individualized proof even where aggregate evidence reveals a major racial disparity.
* **Relationship to Title VII**
  * If **Washington v. Davis** had adopted the **Griggs** framework, the Baldus evidence might have shifted the burden to Georgia to show that its system was not operating through racial discrimination.
  * Because constitutional doctrine leaves the burden on the plaintiff to prove purpose, the professor viewed a victory for McCleskey as highly unlikely after **Washington v. Davis**.

**Grooming Rules and Natural Black Hairstyles: Equal Protection Hypothetical**

* **Supplied Facts**
  * A university maintains facially neutral faculty clothing and grooming rules.
  * One rule prohibits wearing hair in cornrows, locks, or twists.
  * A Black female faculty member challenges the hairstyle restriction as racially discriminatory; the classroom analysis focused only on race, not gender.
  * The faculty member has a professional appearance, wears neat and natural hairstyles, and has a record of professional success.
* **Plaintiff’s Analysis**
  1. Characterize cornrows, locks, and twists as a **proxy for race** or culture rather than merely a neutral grooming category.
  1. Establish **disparate impact** because the prohibition disproportionately affects Black people.
  1. Argue that the university’s claimed interest in professionalism is **pretextual** because the prohibited hairstyles can be neat and professional.
  1. Use the faculty member’s professional success to rebut any assertion that the hairstyle interferes with competent or professional teaching.
  1. Argue that the university could regulate genuinely disruptive hair through less discriminatory standards, such as requiring hair to be neat or kept away from the face, rather than naming hairstyles associated with Black people.
  1. Invoke Justice Stevens’s reasoning that an extreme and foreseeable disparity can support an inference of intent, while recognizing that this is not the governing majority rule.
* **University’s Analysis**
  1. Characterize the policy as a facially neutral **grooming classification**, not a racial classification.
  1. Assert an institutional interest in maintaining professional standards for university teaching.
  1. Emphasize that the text contains no reference to race and supplies no direct evidence of a discriminatory purpose.
  1. Argue under **Palmer v. Thompson** that the policy applies to everyone: no faculty member of any race may wear the listed hairstyles.
  1. Introduce evidence that people who are not Black also wear cornrows or locks, supporting the claim that the policy does not exclusively burden Black individuals.
* **Likely Conclusion**
  * The rule probably has a **disparate impact** on Black individuals, but that alone does not establish an **equal protection** violation.
  * A plaintiff would need persuasive evidence that the university adopted or maintained the rule because of its effect on Black people.
  * Existing courts have not been receptive to constitutional grooming-discrimination claims, and the lecture stated that no **equal protection** challenge to the referenced grooming decision has succeeded.
  * The transcript referred to that decision as “Grimm v. HRC,” but the case name or citation is uncertain due to apparent transcription error.
* **Legislative Response**
  * California and approximately two dozen other states have enacted **CROWN Acts** protecting against discrimination based on hairstyle, including natural Black hairstyles.
  * The professor gave inconsistent counts—California plus either 23 or 24 other states—but summarized the coverage as about half the states.
  * A federal **CROWN Act** was reintroduced in Congress at the end of the preceding year but, as described in the lecture, remained a bill rather than enacted national law.
  * These statutes address a form of discrimination for which constitutional **equal protection** litigation has not been successful.
